pos: n. (proper, a poetic name of Israel; Hebrew, the upright one)
etymology: Hebrew Yeshuruwn, a diminutive of endearment from yashar, upright — little upright one. It occurs three times in the songs of Moses and once in Isaiah, and it is the name God uses for Israel when he is speaking most tenderly and most severely.
biblical_def: The name is used first in an indictment, and the tenderness in it makes the charge worse: “But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation” (Deuteronomy 32:15). The upright one grew fat on God's own bounty and used the strength to kick. Then the blessing: “And he was king in Jeshurun, when the heads of the people and the tribes of Israel were gathered together” (Deuteronomy 33:5) — God himself reigning over the assembly. And the last verse of that blessing: “There is none like unto the God of Jeshurun, who rideth upon the heaven in thy help, and in his excellency on the sky” (Deuteronomy 33:26). Isaiah uses it once more, promising the Spirit poured upon the seed. God calls his people upright not because they are, but because he has determined they shall be.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a poetical and endearing title of Israel, signifying the upright one.
webster_full: UPRIGHT, a. Erect; perpendicular; and figuratively, honest; just; adhering to rectitude in all social intercourse.
ENDEARMENT, n. The act of endearing, or state of being endeared; that which excites or increases affection.
KICK, v.i. To strike with the foot; and figuratively, to spurn; to reject with scorn or contumely.
PROSPERITY, n. Advance or gain in anything good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise.
ROCK, n. In Scripture, a figure of God as a defence, a refuge, and the firm foundation of his people.
scriptures: But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.
And he was king in Jeshurun, when the heads of the people and the tribes of Israel were gathered together.
There is none like unto the God of Jeshurun, who rideth upon the heaven in thy help, and in his excellency on the sky.
Thus saith the LORD that made thee, and formed thee from the womb, which will help thee; Fear not, O Jacob, my servant; and thou, Jesurun, whom I have chosen.
corruption_summary: Prosperity is sought as a sign of God's favour and treated as spiritually neutral, where Deuteronomy 32 names abundance as the very thing that made Jeshurun kick and forsake the God who made him.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 32:15 is the Bible's classic account of what plenty does to a people, and the verbs are brutal: waxed fat, and kicked. The picture is a well-fed animal turning on the hand that fed it. Three clauses pile up the abundance — waxen fat, grown thick, covered with fatness — and then two clauses state the result: he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation. Nothing had gone wrong with the circumstances. The circumstances were the danger, and Moses had warned about it two chapters earlier: when thou hast eaten and art full, beware lest thou forget the LORD.

The other uses guard against reading this as gloom about God's goodness. He is king in Jeshurun when the heads of the people are gathered; there is none like unto the God of Jeshurun, who rideth upon the heaven in thy help. The problem is never the gift; it is the receiver's forgetting. And the name itself is grace: God calls a people who kicked him the upright one, a diminutive of affection, because he sees them as what his covenant will make them. Isaiah uses it while promising to pour water on him that is thirsty and his Spirit upon their seed.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yeshuruwn (H3484), the upright one; yashar (H3477), straight, upright; shamen (H8080), to grow fat; tsuwr (H6697), a rock.

Hebrew yashar (H3477) — straight, right, upright; the root of the name.

“And he was king in Jeshurun” — God reigning over the assembly.
“There is none like unto the God of Jeshurun” — the last word of the blessing.

pos: n. (proper, a prince of Judah; Hebrew, the LORD has saved)
etymology: Hebrew Howshayah, from yasha, to save, and Yah — Jehovah has saved. Two men: a prince who walked in Nehemiah's dedication procession, and the father of two men who refused Jeremiah's word.
biblical_def: At the dedication of the wall, Nehemiah set two great companies of them that gave thanks to go in opposite directions upon it: “And after them went Hoshaiah, and half of the princes of Judah” (Nehemiah 12:32). The other Hoshaiah is known only through his sons at the worst moment of Judah's history. After Gedaliah's murder the remnant came to Jeremiah: “Then all the captains of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least even unto the greatest, came near” (Jeremiah 42:1), and asked him to pray, swearing they would obey whatever answer came. Ten days later God's answer was: abide in this land. And the record of their response is one of the saddest verses in the prophets: “Then spake Azariah the son of Hoshaiah, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the proud men, saying unto Jeremiah, Thou speakest falsely” (Jeremiah 43:2). They went to Egypt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a prince of Judah in Nehemiah's dedication, and as the father of Azariah and Jezaniah in Jeremiah 42 and 43.
webster_full: DEDICATION, n. The act of consecrating to a divine Being, or to a sacred use; solemn appropriation.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
PRESUMPTION, n. Unreasonable confidence; arrogance; blind or headstrong confidence in one's own judgment.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God; an act by which a person binds himself to perform some act.
PROUD, a. Having inordinate self-esteem; possessing a high or unreasonable conceit of one's own excellence.
scriptures: And after them went Hoshaiah, and half of the princes of Judah,
Then all the captains of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least even unto the greatest, came near,

Then spake Azariah the son of Hoshaiah, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the proud men, saying unto Jeremiah, Thou speakest falsely: the LORD our God hath not sent thee to say, Go not into Egypt to sojourn there:
Then they said to Jeremiah, The LORD be a true and faithful witness between us, if we do not even according to all things for the which the LORD thy God shall send thee to us.
corruption_summary: Guidance is sought as confirmation of a decision already made, and Jeremiah 42 is the classic case: men who swore to obey whatever answer came, and called the prophet a liar when it came.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 42 records the most complete promise of obedience in the Old Testament and the swiftest breach of it. The LORD be a true and faithful witness between us, if we do not even according to all things for the which the LORD thy God shall send thee to us. Whether it be good, or whether it be evil, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God. Ten days pass. The answer comes: abide in this land, and I will build you and not pull you down. And Azariah the son of Hoshaiah, Johanan and all the proud men say to Jeremiah, Thou speakest falsely. They had decided on Egypt before they asked.

The pattern is entirely modern. A man seeks counsel, prays for direction, opens the Scriptures — with a conclusion already fixed — and rejects every answer that is not the one he came for, usually by questioning the messenger rather than the message. The test of whether guidance is genuinely being sought is what happens when the answer is unwelcome. The other Hoshaiah in Scripture is walking on a rebuilt wall at the head of half the princes of Judah, giving thanks; the two are what obedience and presumption look like a few generations apart.

pos: n. (proper, a Levite teacher; also one of the crowned men of Zechariah 6)
etymology: Hebrew Towbiyah, from towb, good, and Yah — Jehovah is good. Two men bear it: a Levite whom Jehoshaphat sent through Judah to teach, and one of the exiles whose gift furnished the crowns of Zechariah's great sign.
biblical_def: Jehoshaphat sent a teaching commission through every city of Judah with the book of the law: “And with them he sent Levites, even Shemaiah, and Nethaniah, and Zebadiah, and Asahel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehonathan, and Adonijah, and Tobijah, and Tobadonijah, Levites” (2 Chronicles 17:8). The other Tobijah appears in one of the most remarkable acted prophecies in Scripture. Zechariah is told: “Take of them of the captivity, even of Heldai, of Tobijah, and of Jedaiah, which are come from Babylon, and come thou the same day, and go into the house of Josiah the son of Zephaniah” (Zechariah 6:10), and from their silver and gold to make crowns and set them on the head of Joshua the high priest, and to say, Behold the man whose name is The BRANCH, who shall build the temple of the LORD, and shall be a priest upon his throne. Then: “And the crowns shall be to Helem, and to Tobijah, and to Jedaiah... for a memorial in the temple of the LORD” (Zechariah 6:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as one of the Levites Jehoshaphat sent to teach in Judah, and as one of the returned exiles whose gift made Zechariah's crowns.
webster_full: CROWN, n. An ornament worn on the head by kings and sovereign princes, as a badge of imperial or regal power.
BRANCH, n. In Scripture, a title of the Messiah, the shoot out of the stem of Jesse.
MEMORIAL, n. That which preserves the memory of something; anything that serves to keep in memory.
CATECHIZE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.
TYPE, n. In theology, a figure or representation of something to come; a prefiguration.
scriptures: And with them he sent Levites, even Shemaiah, and Nethaniah, and Zebadiah, and Asahel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehonathan, and Adonijah, and Tobijah, and Tobadonijah, Levites; and with them Elishama and Jehoram, priests.
Take of them of the captivity, even of Heldai, of Tobijah, and of Jedaiah, which are come from Babylon, and come thou the same day, and go into the house of Josiah the son of Zephaniah;
And the crowns shall be to Helem, and to Tobijah, and to Jedaiah, and to Hen the son of Zephaniah, for a memorial in the temple of the LORD.

Even he shall build the temple of the LORD; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.
corruption_summary: The offices of priest and king are kept apart in Israel by law and united only in one man; Zechariah's crowns on a priest's head are the sign of it, and the chapter is often read as anything but that.
corruption_paragraphs: Under the law the two offices were rigorously separate, and Uzziah was struck with leprosy for crossing the line. Zechariah 6 deliberately crosses it under God's own instruction: crowns made from exiles' gold, set on the head of Joshua the high priest, with the declaration Behold the man whose name is The BRANCH... he shall build the temple of the LORD; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both. No mere high priest could be that. The sign points past Joshua to the one who is both, and Hebrews takes it up in the priesthood after the order of Melchizedek.

The homely detail is that the crowns were funded by three men just back from Babylon — Heldai, Tobijah and Jedaiah — and afterwards hung in the temple as a memorial to them. The other Tobijah spent his life going from town to town in Judah with the book of the law, teaching. A name that means Jehovah is good is attached to a man who taught the law and to a man whose silver became a sign of the Priest-King. Neither man did anything spectacular; both are in the Bible because of what they gave to the work of God.

pos: n. (proper, several men; Hebrew, God has helped)
etymology: Hebrew Azarel, from azar, to help, and El, God — God has helped. At least five men bear it: a Korhite warrior at Ziklag, a temple musician, and men of the restoration.
biblical_def: He is first a soldier, among the Korhites who came to David at Ziklag while he was yet kept close because of Saul: “Elkanah, and Jesiah, and Azareel, and Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korhites” (1 Chronicles 12:6). He is next a musician in the courses David and the captains of the host separated to prophesy with harps, psalteries and cymbals: “The eleventh to Azareel, he, his sons, and his brethren, were twelve” (1 Chronicles 25:18) — twenty-four courses of twelve, chosen by lot, the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar. And he is finally a name in the register of those who had taken strange wives and put them away: “Azareel, and Shelemiah, Shemariah” (Ezra 10:41). Soldier, singer, penitent. The name confesses the same thing in every station: God has helped.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of a Korhite warrior, a chief of the eleventh course of temple musicians, and men of the restoration.
webster_full: HELP, v.t. To aid; to assist; to lend strength or means towards effecting a purpose.
COURSE, n. Order of succession; the order in which the priests and singers ministered by turns in the temple.
LOT, n. That which, in human speech, is called chance or hazard, but in Scripture is determined by God.
CYMBAL, n. A musical instrument used by the ancients, consisting of two plates of brass struck together.
PROPHESY, v.i. To utter predictions; and in the Chronicles, to sing praise under the direction of the Spirit.
scriptures: Elkanah, and Jesiah, and Azareel, and Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korhites,
The eleventh to Azareel, he, his sons, and his brethren, were twelve:
And they cast lots, ward against ward, as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar.
corruption_summary: Place and prominence in the church are commonly distributed by influence and self-advancement; the twenty-four courses of singers were assigned by lot, with the small as well as the great, the teacher as the scholar.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Chronicles 25:8 describes a procedure the modern church would find almost unthinkable: And they cast lots, ward against ward, as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar. Twenty-four courses of twelve singers, and the order in which they served — Azareel is the eleventh — was settled by lot rather than by seniority, reputation or negotiation. The lot is cast into the lap, says Proverbs, but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD. Removing human calculation from the assignment removed most of the occasion for ambition at a stroke.

The wider principle is that God assigns place. The New Testament does not direct churches to cast lots for office — after Pentecost the pattern is prayer, examined qualification and the laying on of hands — but it teaches the same conviction: God hath set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him. A man named God has helped appears in Scripture as a soldier, as the eleventh of twenty-four singers, and among men confessing sin. In each case the help was God's and the station was assigned, and neither fact depended on how the man felt about his place in the list.

pos: n. (proper, of the line of David after the exile; Hebrew, servant of the LORD)
etymology: Hebrew Nearyah, from naar, a youth or servant, and Yah — servant of Jehovah. One man of the name stands in the royal line after the captivity; another is a Simeonite captain.
biblical_def: He is in the Davidic genealogy's final stretch: “And the sons of Shechaniah; Shemaiah: and the sons of Shemaiah; Hattush, and Igeal, and Bariah, and Neariah, and Shaphat, six” (1 Chronicles 3:22), and his own sons are counted: “And the sons of Neariah; Elioenai, and Hezekiah, and Azrikam, three” (1 Chronicles 3:23). This is the line of David carried forward in a people with no throne, counted son by son and numbered at the end of each verse. The other Neariah is a Simeonite captain in a raid that is easy to miss: “And some of them, even of the sons of Simeon, five hundred men, went to mount Seir, having for their captains Pelatiah, and Neariah, and Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi” (1 Chronicles 4:42). They smote the remnant of the Amalekites that were escaped, and dwelt there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a descendant of David after the captivity, and as one of four Simeonite captains who went to mount Seir.
webster_full: GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor.
SERVANT, n. A person, male or female, that attends another for the purpose of performing menial offices for him.
LINEAGE, n. Race; progeny; descendants in a line from a common progenitor.
CAPTAIN, n. A head or chief officer; the military officer who commands a company.
EXPECTATION, n. The act of expecting; the state of waiting for or looking for an event to come.
scriptures: And the sons of Shechaniah; Shemaiah: and the sons of Shemaiah; Hattush, and Igeal, and Bariah, and Neariah, and Shaphat, six.
And the sons of Neariah; Elioenai, and Hezekiah, and Azrikam, three.
And some of them, even of the sons of Simeon, five hundred men, went to mount Seir, having for their captains Pelatiah, and Neariah, and Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi.
And they smote the rest of the Amalekites that were escaped, and dwelt there unto this day.
corruption_summary: A promise long unfulfilled is assumed to have lapsed, and the Chronicler answers by counting David's descendants name by name in a kingdom that had no king.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle in these verses is the persistence of a promise. God had sworn to David that his seed should endure for ever and his throne as the sun. By the time the Chronicler wrote, Jerusalem had fallen, the throne was gone, and the line of David was a list of private citizens in a Persian province. And the Chronicler counts them: six sons here, three sons there, the number written at the end of each verse as if it were the muster roll of an army. Somebody was keeping track, because the promise had not lapsed.

The other Neariah's raid supplies a small companion note. Four Simeonite captains took five hundred men to mount Seir and smote the rest of the Amalekites that were escaped, and dwelt there unto this day. Saul had been commanded to destroy Amalek and had spared them; centuries later a handful of obscure men finished what a king had left undone. God's purposes are not abandoned when the prominent fail them. They are carried on, usually by people whose names appear once, in a chapter most readers skip.

pos: n. (proper, son of Eliezer the son of Moses; Hebrew, the LORD has enlarged)
etymology: Hebrew Rechabyah, from rachab, to be wide or enlarged, and Yah — Jehovah has enlarged. He is the only son of Eliezer, who was the second son of Moses, and the note attached to him is a quiet marvel.
biblical_def: The Chronicler is recording the Levitical houses and pauses over Moses' own descendants: “And the sons of Eliezer were, Rehabiah the chief. And Eliezer had none other sons; but the sons of Rehabiah were very many” (1 Chronicles 23:17) — the margin reads were highly multiplied. One son, and from that one son a multitude. He appears again in the courses: “Concerning Rehabiah: of the sons of Rehabiah, the first was Isshiah” (1 Chronicles 24:21), and among the keepers of the treasures: “And his brethren by Eliezer; Rehabiah his son, and Jeshaiah his son, and Joram his son, and Zichri his son, and Shelomith his son” (1 Chronicles 26:25). Eliezer was named by Moses because The God of my father, said he, was mine help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh. His grandson bears a name meaning God has enlarged, and the text says the family was highly multiplied.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the only son of Eliezer the son of Moses, whose own sons were very many.
webster_full: ENLARGE, v.t. To make greater in quantity or dimensions; to extend in limits, breadth or size; to increase.
MULTIPLY, v.i. To increase in number; to extend; to grow or become more numerous by propagation.
POSTERITY, n. Descendants; children, children's children, and so on indefinitely.
TREASURY, n. A place or building in which stores of wealth are reposited; the place where the public revenues are deposited.
OBSCURITY, n. A state of being unknown to fame; a humble condition; privacy.
scriptures: And the sons of Eliezer were, Rehabiah the chief. And Eliezer had none other sons; but the sons of Rehabiah were very many. the
Concerning Rehabiah: of the sons of Rehabiah, the first was Isshiah.
And his brethren by Eliezer; Rehabiah his son, and Jeshaiah his son, and Joram his son, and Zichri his son, and Shelomith his son.
And the name of the other was Eliezer; for the God of my father, said he, was mine help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh: Eliezer: that is, My God is an help
corruption_summary: Significance is measured by what a man leaves that bears his own name; Moses' sons appear only in a Levitical list, and the line runs on through one grandson whom nobody remembers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The striking thing about Rehabiah is whose grandson he is. Moses had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, and neither succeeded him in anything. The leadership went to Joshua, the priesthood to Aaron's line, and Moses' own descendants appear in Chronicles as ordinary Levites over the treasures. There is no dynasty. Whatever else the greatest prophet of the Old Testament left behind, it was not a family office, and the Holy Ghost records the fact without a syllable of complaint.

What was given instead is in the verse itself. Eliezer had none other sons — a single line, easily broken — but the sons of Rehabiah were very many, and the Hebrew margin says highly multiplied. Eliezer's own name means my God is an help, given because God had delivered Moses from Pharaoh's sword. Rehabiah's means God has enlarged. From a narrow place God made room. A household reduced to one son is not a household God has finished with, and the record of Moses' line is the proof.

pos: n. (proper, several men of Judah and Simeon; Hebrew, my salvation)
etymology: Hebrew Yishiy, from yesha, salvation — my salvation, or saving. A separate Hebrew word spelled the same way in English, iyshiy, means my husband, and is the word God promises Israel shall call him in Hosea 2:16.
biblical_def: The name belongs to at least three men in the registers of Judah and Simeon. “And the sons of Appaim; Ishi. And the sons of Ishi; Sheshan. And the children of Sheshan; Ahlai” (1 Chronicles 2:31) — a line that continues through a daughter married to an Egyptian servant, because Sheshan had no sons. “And the sons of Ishi were, Zoheth, and Benzoheth” (1 Chronicles 4:20). And he is the father of the four captains who took mount Seir: “having for their captains Pelatiah, and Neariah, and Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi” (1 Chronicles 4:42). The English spelling collides with a different Hebrew word in one of the tenderest verses in the prophets: “And it shall be at that day, saith the LORD, that thou shalt call me Ishi; and shalt call me no more Baali” (Hosea 2:16) — my husband, and no longer my master.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of men in the registers of Judah and Simeon, and separately as the Hebrew word rendered my husband in Hosea 2:16.
webster_full: SALVATION, n. The redemption of man from the bondage of sin and liability to eternal death, by the atonement of Christ.
HUSBAND, n. A man contracted or joined to a woman by marriage; a correlative term to wife.
MASTER, n. A director; a governor; one who rules or directs; a lord or owner.
BAAL, n. The chief male deity of the Phoenicians and Canaanites; a name signifying lord or master.
BETROTH, v.t. To contract to any one, in order to a future marriage; to affiance.
scriptures: And the sons of Appaim; Ishi. And the sons of Ishi; Sheshan. And the children of Sheshan; Ahlai.
And the sons of Shimon were, Amnon, and Rinnah, Benhanan, and Tilon. And the sons of Ishi were, Zoheth, and Benzoheth.
And some of them, even of the sons of Simeon, five hundred men, went to mount Seir, having for their captains Pelatiah, and Neariah, and Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi.
And it shall be at that day, saith the LORD, that thou shalt call me Ishi; and shalt call me no more Baali.
corruption_summary: God is related to either as a distant master to be placated or as a companion with no authority; Hosea 2:16 promises a people who will call him Ishi, my husband, and no more Baali, my master.
corruption_paragraphs: Hosea 2:16 is a single verse that corrects two opposite errors at once. To a nation that had been calling God Baali — my master, in a word indistinguishable from the name of the idol they had been worshipping — God promises a day when they will call him Ishi, my husband. Servile religion, which deals with God as a proprietor to be kept satisfied, is not what he is after; he is after a covenant of affection, and the verses around it use the language of betrothal: I will betroth thee unto me for ever, in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies.

The safeguard against sentimentality is in the same chapter, which is one of the most severe in the prophets — a wife pursued after her lovers, hedged up with thorns, stripped and left in the wilderness, and only then allured and spoken to comfortably. The intimacy promised is on the far side of judgment, not instead of it. And the change is in the name a people use for God, which is always a good measure of what they actually believe about him. The registers of Chronicles carry the same three letters as a plain personal name: my salvation.

pos: n. (proper, several men; Hebrew, the LORD is gracious)
etymology: Hebrew Yehowchanan, from Yah and chanan, to be gracious — Jehovah is gracious. It is the full form of the name that shortens to Johanan and comes into Greek as John.
biblical_def: He appears first among the sons of Obededom, who were porters at the house of God: “Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Elioenai the seventh” (1 Chronicles 26:3) — a household God had blessed while the ark lodged there. Another Jehohanan is the father of one of the five captains Jehoiada took into covenant to crown the boy Joash: “And in the seventh year Jehoiada strengthened himself, and took the captains of hundreds, Azariah the son of Jeroham, and Ishmael the son of Jehohanan” (2 Chronicles 23:1). A third heads a priestly house after the return: “Of Ezra, Meshullam; of Amariah, Jehohanan” (Nehemiah 12:13). The name is the same one carried by the forerunner, whose father was told by Gabriel to call him John; and Zacharias, when his mouth was opened, prophesied of the tender mercy of our God whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the full form of Johanan, borne by a porter of the house of God, a captain's father, and a priest.
webster_full: GRACIOUS, a. Favorable; kind; friendly; disposed to forgive offences and impart unmerited blessings.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favor of God; the divine influence which renews the heart.
PORTER, n. A man that has the charge of a door or gate; a doorkeeper.
COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons; in Scripture, God's engagement with his people.
FORERUNNER, n. A messenger sent before to give notice of the approach of another; a harbinger.
scriptures: Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Elioenai the seventh.

And in the seventh year Jehoiada strengthened himself, and took the captains of hundreds, Azariah the son of Jeroham, and Ishmael the son of Jehohanan, and Azariah the son of Obed, and Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri, into covenant with him.
Of Ezra, Meshullam; of Amariah, Jehohanan;
But the angel said unto him, Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John.
corruption_summary: Grace is spoken of as a quality of the divine temperament rather than a name a people carried, and the Hebrew habit of embedding doctrine in a child's name is largely lost.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The observation worth making is how common this name is. Jehohanan, Johanan, Hananiah, Hanan, Elhanan, Baalhanan — the root chanan, to be gracious, runs through the registers of Israel like a refrain, and every household that used one of them was confessing something. The doctrine of grace was not first stated in a Latin treatise; it was carried in Hebrew nurseries for a thousand years before Paul wrote about it, in names parents chose because they believed God deals with men on terms they have not earned.

The line ends in the gospel. Gabriel told Zacharias that his son should be called John — the same name in its shortest form, Jehovah is gracious — and the old priest, struck dumb for unbelief and loosed at the naming, prophesied of the dayspring from on high visiting them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death. Every Jehohanan in Chronicles, Nehemiah and Ezra carried that confession as a label. One man in Luke carried it as an office, and went before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.

pos: n. (proper, a nephew of Abraham; also a prince of Ephraim and a Levite)
etymology: Hebrew Qemuwel, probably raised of God or congregation of God. Three men bear it, spread across the whole of Israel's history: a son of Nahor, a prince who helped divide the land, and the father of a Levitical ruler under David.
biblical_def: He appears first in the notice brought to Abraham after the binding of Isaac: “Huz his firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel the father of Aram” (Genesis 22:21). The second Kemuel is appointed to a task of great practical weight — the division of Canaan among the tribes — as one of the princes named by God to Moses: “And the prince of the tribe of the children of Ephraim, Kemuel the son of Shiphtan” (Numbers 34:24). The third is in David's administration: “Of the Levites, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel: of the Aaronites, Zadok” (1 Chronicles 27:17). Genesis 22:20 introduces the first list with a striking phrase — it was told Abraham, saying, Behold, Milcah, she hath also born children unto thy brother Nahor — news of a distant family, given to a man who had just been asked for his only son, and containing in its last line the grandmother of Rebekah.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a son of Nahor and father of Aram, as a prince of Ephraim, and as the father of a Levitical ruler.
webster_full: CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things; in Scripture, the whole body of the people of Israel.
PRINCE, n. A sovereign; the chief of a tribe or family; one invested with authority.
DIVIDE, v.t. To part or separate an entire thing; to distribute; to deal out in shares.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir; the portion of a tribe in the land.
TIDINGS, n. News; advice; information; intelligence; account of what has taken place.
scriptures: Huz his firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel the father of Aram,
And the prince of the tribe of the children of Ephraim, Kemuel the son of Shiphtan.
Of the Levites, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel: of the Aaronites, Zadok:
And it came to pass after these things, that it was told Abraham, saying, Behold, Milcah, she hath also born children unto thy brother Nahor;
corruption_summary: God's provision is expected to arrive as a dramatic intervention, and Genesis 22 records it arriving as family news from a distant country, mentioned in a list of names.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Look at where Genesis puts this list. Abraham has just come down from Moriah, where he had bound his only son and heard the voice from heaven and named the place Jehovah-jireh. And then: And it came to pass after these things, that it was told Abraham, saying, Behold, Milcah, she hath also born children unto thy brother Nahor — Huz, Buz, Kemuel, and five more, and at the end of the list, Bethuel begat Rebekah. The wife for the son whose life had just been given back is announced, unheralded, in a piece of family news from four hundred miles away.

Providence generally works like that. The great intervention on the mountain is followed by an ordinary letter from relatives, and the second is as much God's provision as the first. The other men named Kemuel carried out equally unglamorous appointments — dividing an inheritance among tribes, ruling a division of Levites — and God named them to Moses individually for the task. The believer who is waiting for God to act in a manner he will find unmistakable should read Genesis 22:20 and consider what arrived in the post.

pos: n. (proper, a Benjamite of Jerusalem; also a priest)
etymology: Hebrew Calluw, probably weighed or lifted up. The name belongs to the head of a Benjamite house that settled in Jerusalem after the captivity, and to a chief of the priests in the days of Jeshua.
biblical_def: His pedigree is given twice, at different lengths. The Chronicler: “And of the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hasenuah” (1 Chronicles 9:7). Nehemiah, in the chapter about who would live in the rebuilt city, traces him seven generations: “And these are the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Joed, the son of Pedaiah, the son of Kolaiah, the son of Maaseiah, the son of Ithiel, the son of Jesaiah” (Nehemiah 11:7). A Sallu also heads a priestly course: “Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, Jedaiah. These were the chief of the priests and of their brethren in the days of Jeshua” (Nehemiah 12:7). Nehemiah 11 is the chapter in which the rulers dwelt at Jerusalem and the rest cast lots to bring one of ten to dwell there, and the people blessed all the men that willingly offered themselves to dwell in Jerusalem.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the head of a Benjamite house dwelling in Jerusalem after the captivity, and as a chief of the priests.
webster_full: VOLUNTEER, n. A person who enters into military or other service of his own free will.
LOT, n. That by which the fate or portion of one is determined; in Scripture, disposed of by the LORD.
DWELL, v.i. To abide as a permanent resident; to have a habitation for some time or permanence.
SETTLE, v.i. To become fixed or permanent; to establish a residence; to plant with inhabitants.
WILLING, a. Free to do or grant; having the mind inclined; disposed; not averse.
scriptures: And of the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hasenuah,
And these are the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Joed, the son of Pedaiah, the son of Kolaiah, the son of Maaseiah, the son of Ithiel, the son of Jesaiah.
Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, Jedaiah. These were the chief of the priests and of their brethren in the days of Jeshua.
And the people blessed all the men, that willingly offered themselves to dwell at Jerusalem.
corruption_summary: Where a household lives is treated as a purely economic decision, and Nehemiah 11 records a congregation blessing the men who willingly offered themselves to live in a hard, half-built city because God's house was there.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 11 is a chapter about a housing problem with a spiritual centre. The wall was up and the city was largely empty: the city was large and great, but the people few therein, and the houses were not builded. So the rulers dwelt at Jerusalem, the rest cast lots to bring one of ten to live there, and then comes verse 2: And the people blessed all the men, that willingly offered themselves to dwell at Jerusalem. Moving into a rubble-strewn city with no economy was the costly, unglamorous thing on which the whole restoration depended, and the congregation blessed the men who did it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that where a family settles is a spiritual decision. Lot chose the plain of Jordan because it was well watered everywhere, and pitched his tent toward Sodom. The men of Nehemiah 11 — Sallu heading the Benjamites among them — chose a hard city because the house of God was in it. Congregations are still built by households that move toward a church rather than away from one, and Scripture records the names of the men who did it and the blessing they received.
